# Persistent memory for a local assistant

## Why memory is a separate store

A language model's weights are frozen after training. Anything learned during a
conversation disappears when the process exits unless it is written somewhere.
Persistent memory is that somewhere: a small database of keyed notes that the
assistant can read at the start of a turn and write when the user asks it to
remember something.

Keeping memory separate from the model has three benefits. The user can inspect
and edit it. Updates are immediate, with no retraining. And a mistaken note can
be deleted instead of silently influencing every future answer.

# A minimal tool-calling protocol for a small model

## Why a textual protocol

Large models are often trained with a structured chat template that the serving
stack parses. A small local model can use a simpler approach: tool calls are
ordinary text delimited by special tokens. The model writes a JSON object
between a `<tool_call>` marker and the end of its turn. The runtime parses the
JSON, executes the named tool, and appends the observation after a
`<tool_result>` marker. Nothing about this requires a vendor API.

The format is:

    <tool_call>{"name": "calculator", "arguments": {"expression": "2+2"}}

One JSON object per call, `name` a string, `arguments` an object. Multiple

Retrieval should be conservative. Injecting every note into every prompt wastes
context and increases the chance that an irrelevant fact distracts the model. A
common policy is to search memory with the user's message, take the top two or
three notes, and cap the injected text at a few hundred characters. Notes carry
their updated timestamp so the model can say when a fact was recorded.

## Writing policy

The assistant should write memory only when the user asks it to, or when the
user states a durable preference and confirms it. Facts inferred from a single
ambiguous sentence should not be persisted. Because keys are visible to the
user, they should be short and descriptive: `user_timezone` is better than

# The decoder-only transformer used by TinyLM-50

## Blocks and the residual stream

A decoder-only transformer is a stack of identical blocks operating on a
residual stream of shape (batch, sequence, hidden). Each block applies two
sub-layers, each preceded by normalisation and followed by a residual
addition. Pre-norm placement, where the normalisation is applied to the input
of the sub-layer rather than its output, is easier to train at depth because
the identity path from input to output is never rescaled.

TinyLM-50 uses RMSNorm. RMSNorm divides by the root mean square of the
activations and multiplies by a learned per-feature weight. It omits mean
subtraction, which saves a little work and performs comparably to LayerNorm in
